Description: States directly what the product or service does.
Construction: Combine category noun with modifier or action verb.
Examples: A name meaning 'fast delivery service'; 'online book store'; 'home cleaning app'
Strengths: Immediately clear; easy SEO; no explanation needed
Risks: Generic; hard to protect; limited expansion room
Best For: Utility brands; Everyman archetype; price-competitive categories

Description: Hints at a benefit or quality without stating it literally.
Construction: Choose a word that implies a key attribute through connotation.
Examples: A word evoking speed for a courier; a word evoking clarity for an analytics tool; a word evoking warmth for a care service
Strengths: Distinctive yet meaningful; easier trademark; memorable
Risks: Requires inference; meaning can drift across cultures
Trademark Risk: Medium - implies but does not describe
Best For: Hero and Sage archetypes; premium positioning; brands needing aspiration

Description: A made-up word with no prior dictionary meaning.
Construction: Combine phoneme clusters for desired sound symbolism.
Examples: A two-syllable coined word ending in a vowel; a short sharp invented term; a soft-sounding neologism for a wellness brand
Strengths: Highly protectable; globally portable; no baggage
Risks: Requires heavy investment to build meaning; hard to spell first time
Trademark Risk: Low - no prior use in any category
Best For: Magician and Creator archetypes; global tech brands; categories crossing language borders

Description: Two existing words fused or joined to create a new whole.
Construction: Concatenate or hyphenate two meaningful words.
Examples: A word combining 'open' and 'road' for a travel brand; 'bright' and 'path' for an education platform; 'stone' and 'mark' for a heritage brand
Strengths: Inherits meaning from both parts; recognisable; moderately protectable
Risks: Can feel literal; one half may dominate meaning; long character count
Best For: Explorer and Ruler archetypes; platforms; brands wanting dual positioning

Description: Letters from a longer name or phrase form a short memorable string.
Construction: Take initials of a descriptive phrase or mission statement.
Examples: Three-letter initialism of a professional association name; four-letter acronym of a corporate mission phrase; initialised product suite name
Strengths: Short and type-friendly; easy recall once established
Risks: Meaningless without context; hard to emote; many combinations taken
Trademark Risk: Medium - short strings often already registered
Best For: B2B and institutional brands; Ruler archetype; technical standards bodies

Description: Named after a person - typically a founder or key figure.
Construction: Use surname alone or combined with a category word.
Examples: A brand bearing its founder's surname; a consultancy named 'Hartmann and Partners'; a fashion house named after its designer
Strengths: Immediate credibility and accountability; strong heritage story
Risks: Tied to one person's reputation; hard to sell or rebrand
Trademark Risk: Medium - personal names generally registrable if not already famous
Best For: Caregiver and Sage archetypes; luxury goods; professional services; craft brands

Description: References a real or evocative place name to anchor identity.
Construction: Use a place name - literal or metaphorical - as brand anchor.
Examples: A brand named after a mountain range evoking ruggedness; a coastal city name for a seafood brand; a regional valley name for a wine
Strengths: Instant sense of origin and character; tourism synergy
Risks: Geographically limiting; locals may not find it exotic; registration can conflict
Trademark Risk: High - place names often unregistrable alone
Best For: Explorer and Innocent archetypes; food and beverage; artisan and heritage brands

Description: Borrows a concept from an unrelated domain to transfer its qualities.
Construction: Identify a quality you want then find an unrelated noun that embodies it.
Examples: An animal name chosen for agility; a natural phenomenon chosen for energy; a mythological figure chosen for wisdom
Strengths: Rich meaning transfer; emotionally resonant; distinctive
Risks: Metaphor may not translate culturally; overused domains (animals) feel tired
Trademark Risk: Low to Medium - depends on prior use in category
Best For: Magician and Hero archetypes; challenger brands; brands with a single dominant value

Description: Adopts an existing common word reframed in a new context.
Construction: Take a dictionary word and apply it to an unrelated product category.
Examples: An everyday word meaning 'apple' used for a technology brand; a word for a natural element used for a software tool; a colour word used for a financial service
Strengths: Familiar phonetics; easy to say and spell; memorable
Risks: Descriptive objection risk in some categories; word may carry unwanted associations
Trademark Risk: High - common words are hard to protect without distinctiveness
Best For: Outlaw and Jester archetypes; consumer tech; lifestyle brands wanting approachability

Description: Blends parts of two words into one new word.
Construction: Merge the start of one word with the end (or middle) of another.
Examples: A blend of 'motor' and 'hotel' for roadside lodging; a blend of 'breakfast' and 'lunch' for a meal occasion; a blend of 'web' and 'seminar' for online events
Strengths: Compact; clever; instantly suggests both source concepts
Risks: Feels gimmicky if forced; may read as misspelling; limited language export
Trademark Risk: Low to Medium - blended words are often distinctive
Best For: Creator and Jester archetypes; new category creators; consumer apps

Description: Alters the conventional spelling of a word to gain trademark distinctiveness.
Construction: Substitute a letter or phoneme - often k for c - or remove a vowel.
Examples: A word spelled with 'k' instead of 'c' for a cool brand; a vowel-dropped version of a common adjective; a deliberate double-letter variant
Strengths: Distinctive enough to register; keeps phonetic recognition; social-handle availability
Risks: Confusing in print; perceived as cheap or gimmicky; SEO split
Trademark Risk: Low - altered spelling is usually registrable
Best For: Outlaw and Jester archetypes; youth and lifestyle brands; tech startups needing available domains

Description: Uses a word or number with no semantic link to the product category.
Construction: Choose a word or symbol purely for sound or aesthetic qualities.
Examples: A short word meaning something in one language but chosen for its sound in another; a single digit or numeral as a brand name; a colour name used with no colour product
Strengths: Highly flexible; no limiting associations; protectable
Risks: No built-in meaning cues; expensive to build associations; audience must be told what it is
Trademark Risk: Low - no descriptive link so strong registrability
Best For: Ruler and Magician archetypes; holding companies; brands that will extend across many categories
